findings.claim: Media conglomerates grow through mergers, takeovers and demergers.
findings.truth: Mergers and takeovers can expand a company, but a demerger splits part of a business into a separate business.
findings.evidence: HMRC Business Income Manual BIM82430 says a demerged business is split into two separate parts; AQA spec 3.6.1 lists demergers as a pattern of ownership.

findings.claim: Public service broadcasting is funded by the government or through a licence fee.
findings.truth: Public service broadcasting is defined by its public-service remit, not one funding source. UK public service broadcasters include commercially funded services; Channel 4 Corporation is publicly owned, not-for-profit and funded by commercial revenues.
findings.evidence: AQA spec 3.6.5 distinguishes government-funded, not-for-profit and commercial models. Ofcom, ‘How Ofcom regulates Channel 4’, states that Channel 4 Corporation is funded by commercial revenues and has a public-service remit.

findings.claim: The five UK regulatory bodies named in the specification are: OFCOM, IPSO, BBFC, ASA and PEGI.
findings.truth: The specification names six bodies: OFCOM, IPSO, the Video Standards Council (VSC), BBFC, ASA and PEGI. Recommended: revise the lesson’s regulator set and its five-body prompts to teach the VSC’s UK PEGI-classification role, with matching retrieval content; alternatively, remove any claim that the five named bodies are the complete specification list.
findings.evidence: AQA spec 3.6.7 explicitly names the VSC alongside OFCOM, IPSO, BBFC, ASA and PEGI. GOV.UK, ‘New rules on video game classification’ (27 July 2012), says the VSC classifies games under PEGI.

findings.claim: The watershed is the 9 pm boundary before which adult content should not be broadcast on free-to-air television.
findings.truth: The watershed applies to television, not only free-to-air television. Before 9 pm, material unsuitable for children should not generally be shown.
findings.evidence: Ofcom, ‘Section one: Protecting the under-eighteens’, states that the watershed applies to television and that material unsuitable for children should not generally be shown before 2100.

findings.claim: The Online Safety Act 2023 places duties on large digital platforms to protect users from illegal and harmful content.
findings.truth: The Act places duties on social media companies and search services to protect users from illegal content and children from content harmful to them.
findings.evidence: GOV.UK, ‘Online Safety Act’, states that the Act gives social media companies and search services legal duties to protect users from illegal content and content harmful to children.

findings.claim: Self-regulatory bodies can only require corrections or issue rulings.
findings.truth: Self-regulatory bodies enforce an industry code. Their available sanctions vary; IPSO can require publication of an adjudication and can impose a fine of up to £1 million after a standards investigation.
findings.evidence: IPSO, ‘Monitoring FAQs’, lists publication of an adjudication and fines up to £1 million among its powers after a standards investigation.

summary: Five verified factual corrections are supplied. One specification-scope issue requires a coordinated decision because it affects the lesson’s stated regulator set and related retrieval material.
